# SK1082 — Use the indexer

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`list.ElementAt(i)` is `list[i]`: the language has syntax for the operation the LINQ extension is standing in for.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Modernization |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| ReSharper | `UseIndexedProperty` (`resharper_use_indexed_property_highlighting`) |

## Why

`ElementAt` exists so that a bare `IEnumerable<T>` can be indexed at all — it walks the sequence when it has to and reaches for `IList<T>` when it can. On a `List<T>` the second branch is the only one that ever runs, so the call is a generic entry point wrapped around the indexer the receiver already declares. The indexer is shorter, needs no `using System.Linq`, and says *the collection has positions* rather than *find me the element in that position*, which is the distinction that matters when the next reader asks whether the receiver is a sequence or a list.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
var first = entries.ElementAt(0);
var chosen = entries.ElementAt(index);
```

Write:

```csharp
var first = entries[0];
var chosen = entries[index];
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The receiver is `List<T>` or `ImmutableList<T>` and nothing else, and the reason is the exception the rewrite would otherwise change.** `Enumerable.ElementAt` bounds-checks itself and throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` on every path; `List<T>` and `ImmutableList<T>` throw `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` from their indexers, so on those two the type, and not merely the fact, of the failure survives the rewrite. **An array does not qualify and is the shape this exclusion exists for**: `array.ElementAt(i)` throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` and `array[i]` throws `IndexOutOfRangeException`, so a `catch` written for one stops catching. `ImmutableArray<T>` is excluded for the same reason, and `IList<T>` and `IReadOnlyList<T>` because an array is a legal value for both, which puts the exception type back out of reach. This is the same receiver set as `SK4030`, arrived at from the opposite direction — that rule substitutes one *method* for another and this one removes the call in favour of language syntax. ⚠ `ElementAtOrDefault` is not reported: it returns `default(T)` where the indexer throws, so there is no indexer expression that means the same thing. ⚠ The `Index`-typed `ElementAt(^1)` overload is refused, because `list[^1]` is a different rewrite with a C# 8 floor and is `SK1060`'s subject. ⚠ The call must resolve to `System.Linq.Enumerable`, must be the extension spelling on a receiver rather than the static one, and must not be a conditional access — `xs?.ElementAt(i)` becomes `xs?[i]`, which is a different edit. ⚠ `UseIndexedProperty`'s own shape, an explicit `get_Item` call, is not covered and cannot be: C# rejects a direct accessor call with `CS0571`, so the inspection has no C# source form to report on and this rule takes the reachable half of the concept.
